q7.answer: Each API instance learns of a change either from a watch on the serving config record or from its 15-second poll, whichever comes first. It loads any named version it does not yet hold from the artifact store, warms it with a test inference, then swaps the active pointer in memory, so no restart or redeploy is needed. If the load or warm-up fails, the instance keeps the previous active version and reports the failure.

q8.answer: The shadow model gets its inputs from the feature bundle that the request already read in step 2, which is copied into the shadow event, so both models see identical features and no second store read happens. Shadow stays off the request path because the event is added to a bounded in-memory queue with a non-blocking attempt only after the response has been sent, and a separate worker pool runs the candidate.

q9.answer: If the shadow queue is full or the workers are saturated, the event is dropped and a counter is incremented, and the user's response is unchanged. The shadow sampling rate then reads lower than configured, which the aggregation reports. Shadow calls also have a timeout and a circuit breaker, so a failing candidate cannot back up the pool.

q10.answer: The active model's 20 items are recorded in each shadow queue event, and the candidate's result, with those active items, is written to an append-only shadow results store with user IDs hashed. A daily aggregation compares the two per day and in total, computing candidate error rate, candidate inference p99, overlap at 20 and rank correlation, catalog coverage, and spread across users, alongside an active-path health check in the same window.

q11.answer: A version is blocked at three points: at registration, any required feature missing from the feature catalog marks it ineligible, and the control plane refuses to set an ineligible version as shadow or active. At serving time, step 3 checks each required feature against the bundle and falls back with missing_feature if one is absent, and shadow is skipped with a logged reason when the candidate is ineligible or not loaded.

q12.answer: A rollback is a config write that sets active_version back to the previous version, using the same compare-and-set on revision as any other change, and needs no ML lead approval. That version is still loaded on every instance and still in the registry, so nothing is downloaded; instances apply the change through the config watch or the 15-second poll, which bounds it under one minute, and the control plane confirms the fleet has the new revision within 60 seconds. A popular_only serving mode in the same config record is the last resort.
